subject: Chemistry
question_text: Discuss the pattern of variation in the oxidation states of (i) B to Tl and (ii) C to Pb.
answer_text: (i) The electric configuration of group 13 elements is ns2np1. Therefore, the most common oxidation state exhibited by them should be +3. However, it is only boron and aluminium which practically show the +3 oxidation state. The remaining elements, i.e., Ga, In, Tl, show both the +1 and +3 oxidation states. On moving down the group, the +1 state becomes more stable. For example, Tl (+1) is more stable than Tl (+3). This is because of the inert pair effect. The two electrons present in the s-shell are strongly attracted by the nucleus and do not participate in bonding. This inert pair effect becomes more and more prominent on moving down the group. Hence, Ga (+1) is unstable, In (+1) is fairly stable, and Tl (+1) is very stable. The stability of the +3 oxidation state decreases on moving down the group. (ii) The electronic configuration of group 14 elements is ns2np2. Therefore, the most common oxidation state exhibited by them should be +4. However, the +2 oxidation state becomes more and more common on moving down the group. C and Si mostly show the +4 state. On moving down the group, the higher oxidation state becomes less stable. This is because of the inert pair effect. Thus, although Ge, Sn, and Pb show both the +2 and +4 states, the stability of the lower oxidation state increases and that of the higher oxidation state decreases on moving down the group.
final_answer: Thus, the oxidation states of elements in groups 13 and 14 show a trend of increasing stability of lower oxidation states as we move down the group.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of oxidation states and the inert pair effect.

question_text: How can you explain higher stability of BCl3 as compared to TlCl3?
answer_text: BCl3 is more stable than TlCl3 because the +3 oxidation state of B is more stable than the +3 oxidation state of Tl. In Tl, the +3 state is highly oxidising and it reverts back to the more stable +1 state.
final_answer: Therefore, BCl3 exhibits higher stability compared to TlCl3.
difficulty_reasoning: Involves understanding of oxidation states and stability.

question_text: Why does boron trifluoride behave as a Lewis acid?
answer_text: Boron trifluoride behaves as a Lewis acid because it has three electrons in its valence shell, forming only three covalent bonds, which leaves its octet incomplete. Thus, it remains electron-deficient.
final_answer: Hence, boron trifluoride acts as a Lewis acid.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of Lewis acid-base theory.

subject: chemistry
question_text: What are electron deficient compounds? Are BCl3 and SiCl4 electron deficient species? Explain.
answer_text: In an electron-deficient compound, the octet of electrons is not complete, i.e., the central metal atom has an incomplete octet. Therefore, it needs electrons to complete its octet. BCl3 is an appropriate example of an electron-deficient compound. B has 3 valence electrons. After forming three covalent bonds with chlorine, the number of electrons around it increases to 6. However, it is still short of two electrons to complete its octet. SiCl4 is not an electron-deficient compound as it has a complete octet.
final_answer: Therefore, BCl3 is an electron-deficient compound, while SiCl4 is not.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of electron deficiency and the ability to explain with examples.

question_text: What is the state of hybridisation of carbon in diamond and graphite?
answer_text: The state of hybridisation of carbon in diamond is sp3 hybridised and is bonded to four other carbon atoms. In graphite, each carbon atom is sp2 hybridised and is bound to three other carbon atoms.
final_answer: Therefore, carbon in diamond is sp3 hybridised, while in graphite it is sp2 hybridised.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of hybridisation and structural differences.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Suggest reasons why the B–F bond lengths in BF3 (130 pm) and BF4– (143 pm) differ.

question_image.description: Diagram illustrating the bond lengths in BF3 and BF4-.

answer_text: The B–F bond length in BF3 is shorter than the B–F bond length in BF4–. BF3 is an electron-deficient species. With a vacant p-orbital on boron, the fluorine and boron atoms undergo pπ–pπ back-bonding to remove this deficiency. This imparts a double-bond character to the B–F bond, causing the bond length to shorten in BF3 (130 pm). However, when BF4– coordinates with the fluoride ion, a change in hybridisation from sp2 (in BF3) to sp3 (in BF4–) occurs, leading to the loss of double-bond character and a longer bond length of 143 pm.
final_answer: Thus, the difference in bond lengths is due to the hybridization change and the presence of double-bond character in BF3.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of hybridization and bond character.

subject: chemistry
question_text: If B-Cl bond has a dipole moment, explain why BCl3 molecule has zero dipole moment.
answer_text: As a result of the difference in the electronegativities of B and Cl, the B-Cl bond is polar in nature. However, the BCl3 molecule is non-polar because it is trigonal planar in shape, making it symmetrical. The respective dipole moments of the B-Cl bonds cancel each other, resulting in a zero dipole moment.
final_answer: Therefore, the BCl3 molecule has a zero dipole moment despite the polar B-Cl bonds.

subject: chemistry
question_text: Aluminium trifluoride is insoluble in anhydrous HF but dissolves on addition of NaF. Aluminium trifluoride precipitates out of the resulting solution when gaseous BF3 is bubbled through. Give reasons.
answer_text: Hydrogen fluoride (HF) is a covalent compound and has very strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding, thus it does not provide ions and aluminium fluoride (AlF3) does not dissolve in it. Sodium fluoride (NaF) is an ionic compound, and when added to the mixture, AlF3 dissolves due to the availability of free F– ions. When boron trifluoride (BF3) is added to the solution, aluminium fluoride precipitates out because boron has a greater tendency to form complexes than aluminium, leading to the replacement of Al by B in the complexes.
final_answer: Thus, the addition of NaF allows AlF3 to dissolve, and BF3 causes it to precipitate out.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of solubility and complex formation.

question_text: Suggest a reason as to why CO is poisonous.
answer_text: Carbon monoxide is highly poisonous because of its ability to form a complex with hemoglobin. The CO-Hb complex is more stable than the O-Hb complex, preventing hemoglobin from binding with oxygen, which can lead to suffocation.
final_answer: Thus, CO's stability in forming complexes with hemoglobin makes it dangerous.
difficulty_reasoning: Involves understanding of chemical bonding and biological implications.

question_text: How is excessive content of CO2 responsible for global warming?
answer_text: Carbon dioxide is essential for survival, but excessive CO2 in the atmosphere poses a serious threat. Increased combustion of fossil fuels, decomposition of limestone, and deforestation have led to higher levels of CO2. CO2 traps heat from the sun, and higher levels result in increased atmospheric temperatures, causing global warming.
final_answer: Therefore, the rise in CO2 levels contributes significantly to global warming.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of environmental science and greenhouse effect.

question_text: Explain structures of diborane and boric acid.

parts.answer_text: Diborane (B2H6) is an electron-deficient compound with only 12 electrons - 6 from 6 H atoms and 3 from each of the 2 B atoms. The structure shows 2 boron and 4 terminal hydrogen atoms in one plane, while the other two bridging hydrogen atoms lie in a plane perpendicular to the boron atoms. The terminal bonds are regular two-centre two-electron (2c - 2e-) bonds, while the two bridging (B-H-B) bonds are three-centre two-electron (3c - 2e-) bonds.
parts.final_answer: Thus, diborane has a unique structure due to its electron deficiency and bonding characteristics.

parts.answer_text: Boric acid has a layered structure where each planar BO3 unit is linked to another through H atoms. The H atoms form covalent bonds with a BO3 unit and hydrogen bonds with another BO3 unit.
parts.final_answer: Therefore, boric acid exhibits a layered structure due to hydrogen bonding.

difficulty_reasoning: Involves understanding of molecular structures and bonding.

question_text: How would you explain the lower atomic radius of Ga as compared to Al?
answer_text: Although Ga has one shell more than Al, its size is lesser than Al. This is because of the poor shielding effect of the 3d-electrons. The shielding effect of d-electrons is very poor and the effective nuclear charge experienced by the valence electrons in gallium is much more than it is in the case of Al.
final_answer: Thus, the lower atomic radius of Ga compared to Al is due to the poor shielding effect of 3d-electrons.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of atomic structure and shielding effects.
